utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric -- call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Martinovic and Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness BB, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I have a few additional questions but I first want to take you back to the map, the map that you looked at yesterday. This is -- this is P11.18.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I can ask the usher to please hand it to the witness? Yes. And the copy, please, because the witness is going to mark it. So I don't know whether my learned friends would like to check the copy to see whether it is a copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence map is marked D2/12.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness BB, can I please ask you to take a marker and mark the position of the Health Centre on the copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, perhaps you can give the witness a marker so that he can do his markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please mark it with number 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. Will you now please put number 2 in the area which you described as neighbourhood called Pijesak, where that professor used to live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, this street -- I don't know the old name of the Queen Katarina Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Is that the area next to Zahum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area where the first elementary school was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you mark it with number 2, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you then mark with number 3 the old Zagreb Bank which was then -- which then became a ministry and in front of which you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, just one more mark, number 4, for the school of mechanical engineering.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are done. Oh, yes, one more thing, the Tobacco Institute, which would be number 5 now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you then just place an arrow in the direction where the Tobacco Institute would be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We are done with this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can now ask the usher to get the witness P496. This is from binder 10 of the Prosecution file.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Is there a B/C/S version in there? Is it only an English version or is there also a B/C/S version? The front page should have the heading the "Defence Department Report." Do you have it? It seems that you do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you please read the heading out loud to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "Military Police Administration Report."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Line of readiness."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you then read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: "9th Battalion of the HVO Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Health Centre held by ATG Mrmak."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How about the next page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Aleksica houses held by Benko Penavic."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Next one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: "4th Battalion, 3rd Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Based on this quick reading, do you agree with me that there were several ATGs deployed in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that only one ATG existed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I ever said, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that concludes all our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from Judges? Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have a few questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness BB, I understood you to say at the beginning of your evidence that you had been with an HVO unit until the date on which the Vranica building was attacked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. It was the 4th Battalion, group for maintenance of facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So can I take it that you were not in any way informed that there was going to be an attack on the town of Mostar on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you think that the intelligence of the HVO would have known of your involvement with the Bosniak side in the weeks previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I go on to something different now. You stated that you're a light sleeper, and that for the previous few weeks, there had been a United Nations tank parked fairly near to where the Vranica building is, and it was there because hostilities were rising between the two factions. And yet you said that on that particular morning just prior to the commencement of the attack, the tank seemed to leave the town of Mostar. I find that very, very strange. Is there any explanation for why the United Nations tank would leave the town at the very moment when its presence would be so important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At 3.00, the tank, which was parked at the intersection near the School of Economics, in front of the Vranica, started its engines. It was a quiet night. One could hear it, and it left its position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And I take it that you've never heard any explanation for why the tank should have left at such a crucial time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, you're a local Mostar man, and obviously before the real hostilities started, you would have known the characters who were in the leadership on the Bosniak side and the Croat side. You told us that you knew Mr. Martinovic for 25 years because of sport and so on but that you didn't socialise with him. Did you know the other accused in this case, Mr. Naletilic, Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only by sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So you did know him by sight. I know he came from Siroki Brijeg and he had lived in Germany, but you did know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he came back before the outbreak of hostilities to fight against the Serbian side. He was a frequent visitor to Mostar, went to a well-known restaurant in Bijeli Brijeg, where the others also gathered. I saw him two -- three or four times, because he has a characteristic appearance, and I was told who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: During the aggression or the defence of the town of Mostar and the region against the Serb aggression, did Mr. Naletilic have a military description, according to reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you crossed from the right bank to the left, in order to liberate the area from the Serbs, the army and the Convicts Battalion operated together. That is during the liberation of Mostar. The commander of this battalion was Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So even at the time that the two sides were fighting together, the commander of the battalion was Mr. Naletilic? I just want to be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, being a native of Mostar and understanding the language, the name that has been given to this battalion is the Convicts Battalion. Sometimes it's called the Punishment Battalion. They seem to be used interchangeably. What did you, as a local Mostar resident, understand by the term "Convicts Battalion"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: We understood it - and perhaps this is a little bit harsh to say - that people who were clearing the terrain, and these were the people who would leave everything -- who would clear everything out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In a scorched-earth policy sort of way? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not scorched, but rather cleared of the enemy forces, of the enemy personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That would indicate that they were very tough, but where does the word "convicts" come into this? Did they have to have served a prison sentence? Did they come from jails? Or are we being given a sort of loose translation of the word?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not former convicts. Perhaps some were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So if I understand that in order to be a soldier in Mr. Naletilic's platoon, one had to have served time in jail, I would be incorrect; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You would not be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I would not be right. So can I take it that you would have been aware of the existence of this tough battalion that was good at clearing out the enemy for some time before the attack on Mostar on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, if I bring you to Mr. Martinovic, you said that he was -- first of all, you knew him, and secondly, that his movements were distinctive because of the car that he drove, a pink, American convertible. Was that before the attack on Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It was. Did you associate Mr. Martinovic with any military activity prior to the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first, when the conflict broke out between the Serbs on the one side and the Croats and Muslims on the other side, Mr. Martinovic was a commander of HOS in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We've heard that HOS is a right-wing, Croatian organisation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, both the HOS and HVO and Muslims were all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. So you associated Mr. Naletilic with military activity as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Were you surprised to hear his counsel, Mr. Seric, say that Mr. Naletilic -- sorry, Mr. Martinovic, didn't in fact join the Convicts Battalion until after the attack on Mostar? I think that's the first time this Court has heard that, that he didn't join the Convicts Battalion until after the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the information I have. When the HOS was dissolved, he remained in the HVO units. That is, he joined the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How would you have known that, Witness BB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar, there exists a group who transferred from the HOS to the HVO. They said that their commander was Stela. He was in uniform. That means that he was with units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you know anything about -- I know you were arrested on the 9th. But did you know anything about a particular part of the town being under the control of Martinovic, Stela, the place around the medical centre? Did you know anything at all about that, or did these events occur after you had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You knew nothing about that. Now, if I can bring you to your period of captivity, this Court has heard a great deal about swimming pools. And you pointed out to us in a photograph of the Tobacco Institute in Siroki Brijeg, which appears to be a very, very large installation. In that photograph, we saw -- the sound is very high, isn't it? Is that better? In that photograph, we saw a swimming pool over on the right-hand side of the photograph. From what I heard -- what I understood of your evidence, it was a sort of public or municipal swimming pool that was being repaired. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a municipal pool which had been neglected for ten years. And we went to clean it out, and also the area around the pool for this projected sports centre. And both Jablanica and guards said that it would be shared half and half between Jablanica and Tuta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Where was that swimming pool in relation to Tuta's house that you could partially see through the walls? And then you said you had a better view when you were near the school, you could see the side of it. Where was the swimming pool vis-a-vis that particular house or villa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The swimming pool was directly across from the Tobacco Institute where the Convicts Battalion command headquarters was. And Tuta's house was 5 or 6 kilometres away from that. I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly, but it was that distance from the pool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: A fair distance away. Now, I appreciate that you never worked at Tuta's house but you worked in the near vicinity. Was there a swimming pool at that villa as far as you could see? Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You didn't see. So any swimming pool that you are talking about is the semi-abandoned municipal pool beside the Tobacco Institute. That's the only pool you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, my last question is that you mentioned some torture that you suffered at the hands of Ivan Cikota.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you know anything about his brother who had been killed just prior to these events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that he was a well-known and good fighter in the Convicts Battalion and that he was killed somewhere near Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So you were aware that this Ivan Cikota had a brother whose name might have been, I think, Mario Cikota. You were aware of that? And he was a sort of hero in the Convicts Battalion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry, there's just one important area. Do you remember when you described how you and other prisoners were painting a building at Siroki Brijeg and cleaning the carpets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You described it: a separate building, it's a house, in fact, and you described that as being Tuta's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Who gave you the order to paint that house and to clean the carpets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our guards would only pick out three or four men, whatever they would need, and take us wherever work needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Tuta came there one day to just see how the work was progressing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he was on the ground floor where the offices were. And we were working upstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you have any doubt in your mind that this was Tuta's particular building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't Tuta's house, Tuta's building. It was the headquarters, the command of the Convicts Battalion within the Tobacco Institute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So does that mean that Mr. Andabak would have been there, too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You were telling us that Mr. Andabak, when he introduced himself to you, called himself Tuta's deputy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Colonel Ivan Andabak, Tuta's deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And is that the word that he used, "deputy"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness BB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge Clark's questions? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, only one question. Further Re-examination by Mr. Poriouvaev:

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness BB, could you tell me, during your direct examination, you stated that you had seen Stela in Tuta's headquarters in Siroki Brijeg. Do you remember if he was dressed in military uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. They were standing in front of the building, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to intervene, not to disturb my colleague, but there was no question in cross-examination about the presence of Vinko Martinovic in Siroki Brijeg so this additional question by my learned friend wasn't really necessary. But let's go on. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Seric:

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something remained unclear, Witness BB. I wouldn't like the Trial Chamber to remain confused. I did not try to infer that Vinko Martinovic had left Mostar in my cross-examination, but I just asked you whether Vinko Martinovic joined the Convicts Battalion after the 12th of May, 1993, and then you answered that you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: After the 12th of May, 1993. And yesterday you answered that you were not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I was -- I was arrested after the 10th, and I don't know how the political or the military situation developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to repeat my question as an introduction, and I wanted to make it clear to the Trial Chamber, to make it clear that I wasn't trying to present some sort of theory through my cross-examination. But I hope it is clear now. And you have answered my question. Today, in response to a question by Judge Clark, you said that you knew that Vinko Martinovic was a member of the HOS. Could you tell me, how do you know that? Or let me ask you directly, to make this short. Were you a member of the HOS under Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In your statement of September 1997, you said you were a member of HOS under Vinko Martinovic. Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I rather wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You rather wouldn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: For private reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let's tackle this in another way. Do you know whether there were any Muslims in a large percentage, at that almost 70 per cent, in the HOS unit under Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attitude of Vinko Martinovic towards Muslims in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same, equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: No difference as compared to Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Was it correct -- do you want me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Be so kind as to tell me, if you know, when was the Convicts Battalion established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there when it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that it was set up and got that name as a reference to political prisoners during the communist regime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And are you aware --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Poriouvaev?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object because now the parties are authorised to ask questions emanating from Judge Clark's questions and responses so -- of the witness, but now we are going beyond the questions posed by Judge Clark. So did Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite agree with you in this point but we are very interested to know that, where the Convicts Battalion, the name of that comes from. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So you're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Judge Clark also asked you whether you knew the position of Mr. Naletilic in the war against the Serbs and you said he was commander of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HOS, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Naletilic, I mean.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You mean Stela? I thought Stela. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Who was commander of the staff, commanders of zones, commanders of brigades, divisions at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a civilian in the war against the Serbs. I don't know any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether a recreation centre was ever built at that swimming pool?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no such information. Until October 1993, it wasn't built.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know who gave the order to clear out that pool?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were taken there by the police to do the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No more questions. Was it recorded that the police took them there? Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for giving the evidence. We all wish you good luck. When the usher pulls down the blinds, you can go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at this moment, do you have any documents to tender into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would tender into evidence Documents -- Exhibits P11.18, 16.4 and 16.5 under the seal, 26.9, 26.10, 39.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, how about P14.3?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I wouldn't tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there are some marks made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, there are some marks, but I don't insist on having it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections? Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections, Your Honour. But I would like to tender on behalf of the Defence the map that was marked with numbers by the witness this morning. We got a number D2/12. And this last document which the witness looked at regarding the demarcation line, and that was Exhibit 5496. I would tender it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no objection, because all of these are photographs. The only thing is the Defence would like also to tender the previous statement of this witness or, rather, only its relevant parts. You remember in the previous statement he said he was a member of the BH army, that he didn't see, et cetera, so we are leading that statement, only the relevant parts, and have it translated into English because we really can't keep up with the translation requirements, and we have a lot of work. So we would like to tender the previous statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objections. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. All those documents have been admitted into the evidence. And Madam Registrar will give them proper numbers. As for the Document PP11.18, which has already been admitted into the evidence, now we have the marks made by the witness, so I believe it should be a new number. Yes, before the next witness, there are two things I would like to inform both parties. The first matter is about the Friday afternoon sitting. After consultations with my colleagues, we believe that we have been -- we have some previous appointments of the other obligations on Friday afternoon. So at least in this month, there's no Friday afternoon sitting. There might be some possibilities for next month. The second thing is that this Trial Chamber is seized by the motion filed by Defence counsel to hold a status conference in accordance with Rule 65 bis. We do not think there's any precedent for a status conference being held during the trial on the basis of Rule 65 bis. That rule is meant to ensure that no accused spends more than 120 days in the detention unit without seeing a Judge. However, that does not rule out the possibility for this Trial Chamber to devote some time, mainly on the procedural matters, during the trial. So this Trial Chamber invites both parties, especially the Defence, to provide the Trial Chamber with a list of issues which they intend to raise with this Trial Chamber so that we could make the decision whether we should have this kind of meeting on procedural matters or not. Thank you. Next witness, Mr. Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I'll be handling the next witness. If we can just shift here for a moment, and then I have one or two matters to raise before the witness comes in. Mr. President, just in terms of what you just said, just to clarify, as I understand the Court's statements about the schedule, we would not work Friday afternoon this week. And you said month, and I assume you might have meant week. But there's the question a week from Friday, that is next week Friday afternoon, is still an issue, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There's a possibility. At this stage, I could only say there's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Your Honour, obviously we have to build a plan accordingly, and that determines how many witnesses come and travel from Bosnia or not. We can't do that, of course, on the spur of the moment. So we would ask the Court to give us as much guidance as possible as early as possible. Just to clarify for the record, Your Honour, in terms of the last witness statement that was offered by Mr. Krsnik, we will state a continuing position, a continuing objection to the receipt, as we have said before, to the receipt of statements, witness statements, into evidence as substantive evidence. We understand the practice of having them marked for identification for the record, as they might be considered for purposes of credibility, but we have said since the depositions, and continue to say and it continues to be our position and will continue to be our position, that such statements should not be accepted as substantive evidence. Again, the evidence, we believe, from a witness is the testimony given in the courtroom. And that's our position. I'm not asking for the Chamber to agree. I'm just simply making it for the record so our position is clear. Your Honour, the next witness will be a protected witness. He has asked for a pseudonym and face and voice distortion. I have raised this previously with the staff. Voice distortion, as you may know, does involve some additional complications, but that's what the witness has requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you will allow me this opportunity to respond to my learned friend, to his latest intervention regarding prior statements, I really have to say that I don't understand. And sometimes I'm really in a position in front of this Trial Chamber to -- forced to discuss the system that we are working in, and it seems I don't really understand, and I don't even know the things that I thought I knew. I never thought I had to deal with such things as a lawyer. The prior statements referred to by the Prosecutor, and I want to note that there had been no objection before and now we hear there is one, this is the only time that the Defence in this whole tactics and the phantasm of prior trials, that is the only opportunity we have to check -- to put to the test the credibility of a witness, because if a witness didn't -- wasn't telling the truth in previous trials, then what is the purpose of those witnesses? And it was based on those statements that an indictment was brought. And now the Prosecution is objecting to having this in evidence. I really can't understand. And I contest this most strongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, we are not debating on this issue. Are you going to say something on this very issue? We are not debating here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is on the same issue but not the same thing. I just wanted to let the Trial Chamber know that the Prosecution should be reminded of the Grassberger book, "The Psychology of Penal Proceedings," from the end [sic] of the century, which says clearly that the passage of time affects the credibility of a witness's statements, and we can see this best if we compare previous statements with current ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, no, Mr. Scott, we are not going to spend much time on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I thought you wanted me to call the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have to ask whether there is any objections from the Defence side as for the protective measures. Are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As usual, Your Honours, the Defence has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume Mr. Seric didn't have objection to the protective measures either, just for the record. I don't think there was a response on the record on protective measures from Mr. Seric, as opposed to Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may call your next witness, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, for the record, I repeat my previous position. I'm sorry, Mr. President, you didn't hear me. I don't believe there is anything on the record concerning Mr. Seric's position on protective measures for this witness. I think you only heard from Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will repeat for the record, I agree with protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, this next witness will give testimony concerning or relevant to the following issues, that is background, paragraph 7, 10 and 11; superior authority, paragraphs 14 to 17; general allegations including such matters as international armed conflict and the existence of widespread and systematic behaviour, paragraphs 18 to 21; count 1, persecutions, paragraphs 26, 28, 31, 33, and 34; counts 2 to 5, forced labour, paragraph 44; counts 9 to 12, wilfully causing great suffering, paragraph 45 and 50; and count 21, plunder, paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe there is some problem with the microphone. Would you please check it, Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will inform you now that the Chamber has granted certain protections for you in connection with your testimony, and those are the following: You will testify using what is called a pseudonym, which means that your real name will not be broadcast or be placed on the record. That will be a matter of confidentiality. Also, your facial image as displayed on any sort of broadcast will be distorted so you cannot be seen, and your voice will also be distorted. Now, having said all those things, let me caution you about a couple of things. In order to maintain these protections, I would advise you and caution you not to use -- you might inadvertently tend to use your own name or a family name or mention a close family member which might tend to identify you. So I'm going to caution you not to, if you can think about it, not to do those things to avoid identifying yourself. Also, the voice distortion adds another level of complication to the procedure; that is, I have to turn off my mic after I ask you a question so that the system will function. So that will be more my problem, I suppose, than yours, but just so you know what's happening. That's the procedure that we have to follow. Witness, I've asked if a piece of paper be put in front of you bearing your name. This is so that the record shows your true name. But it will otherwise be completely protected and sealed. So I'm going to ask you now, don't state your name, but will you please look at that piece of paper and say -- answer yes or no, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: His pseudonym is CC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, you just may have heard, may have been translated for you, that the pseudonym or name, if you will, the symbol that's going to be used to refer to you is going to be "CC," that is double "C." So if you hear that, that's the purpose. It's not meant as any sort of disrespect or to cause confusion. You'll be referred to as "Witness CC." Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, I understand that in April -- by way of background -- in April of 1993, you went to the ABiH headquarters in the Vranica building in Mostar, and during those days, joined the ABiH. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Several days later, you went to an ABiH position or facility at that time that was located in Hotel Mostar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, is it true, Witness, that on the 16th of April, there was some shelling of Hotel Mostar. And if the answer is yes, can you just briefly describe what happened in that regard on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April - actually even before, 14th and 15th - one could feel certain tensions. And on the 16th, there was shelling. We were inside. Some were outside, of course. And the shooting started. The shelling started. And as far as I know -- actually, I do know that some shells fell on the surrounding buildings, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. You said tensions were increasing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that tensions were increasing around that time. Did you have personal knowledge of any sort of deadline or ultimatum that had been issued for the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I personally did not know about the ultimatum, but I did see men in black uniform, the so-called HOS. We saw them moving about, and there was tension because we were wondering why the HOS would be passing through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, on the 17th of April, do you recall, that is the next day, do you recall some sort of a cease-fire agreement being signed between the ABiH and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I do remember Mr. Arif Pasalic came and said that there would be an agreement that we had to move from that part of Mostar. But I don't know with whom he reached this agreement. But I know that UNPROFOR was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you say there was an agreement to leave that part of Mostar, are you talking about leaving -- the ABiH leaving Hotel Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And do you know to where that unit was to relocate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I know where I personally transferred. UNPROFOR was moving people and their vehicles. I know that I was transferred to the left bank, to Konak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, if you know, in the days following the 17th of April, 1993, what did you observe in terms of whether the HVO kept or complied with the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I don't know that they completely complied with it, but it was less intensive than -- intense than on the 16th, that is, the shooting on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you recall there continuing to be sniper fire after -- from the HVO side after the 17th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, directing your attention a few days forward, around the 21st or 22nd of April, did you and some other men join the ABiH military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And where were you based -- excuse me. Once you became part of the military police, where were you based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I was based in Semovac, near Hotel Ruza, that is Semovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Apart from your base, and distinguishing where you lived, if you will, and spent the evenings or non-duty hours, what was your duty station at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: When I was on duty, I was at the headquarters in the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention to the 8th of May, were you on duty in the Vranica complex on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: From 2.00 in the afternoon onward, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, when I said just now intentionally "the Vranica complex," was there another building, a part of that complex, which you may refer to, and others, as the logistics building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the logistics building exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber what was the relationship or the proximity between the logistics building or portion of the complex and the Vranica building where the ABiH 4th Corps headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: They were connected. They were linked with a passageway that was sort of like almost like an underpass or something. There were four or five metres from one door to the other. That is not the front door of the Vranica but the back door of the Vranica and the door to the logistics building were in close proximity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that altogether there were about eight soldiers, ABiH soldiers, and three logistics staff in the logistic component of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go into private session for one or two questions concerning the names of others persons, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness CC, I'll repeat my question to you. Directing your attention to the 9th of May, that is the next day, 1993, can you tell the Chamber where you were on that morning and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: When the first shells started falling, I was asleep. And as the shells started falling - now I'm talking about my own experience - I jumped up and it was heavy shelling at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where were you located at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: In the dormitory in the basement. There was a dormitory there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: As we have been discussing in the last few minutes, was that the logistics portion of the complex?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, in the logistics portion of the complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you tell, or were you able to observe, at any point around that time, where the fire was coming from and what kind of fire it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: It was coming -- my feeling was it was coming from all sides. At first, it was shells, the first -- it was all kinds of shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what was happening as the shelling -- just give us a bit of a picture as to what you saw happening around you as the shelling started. What were people doing? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, panic ensued. Civilians were panicked because, of course, if shells are falling, you don't know where they were going to hit. And it took us a while to -- for to us get our bearings. We couldn't get out. One soldier tried to get out and was immediately hit by a sniper. We pulled him back in and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I seem to lose translation. I heard the witness speaking but I didn't hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Everybody ran for cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Around this time, did you ever gain a position or a vantage point where you could look outside the building and see what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, we peeked out the windows where the fire was coming, but you couldn't really determine where they were coming, from Hum, from Goranci; it was coming from all over the place. It was unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did there time come a time when you were able to see individual members of the attacking forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Indirectly, no. But no, I couldn't see if I had seen it. I would have to shoot, too, but I could not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Witness CC, perhaps my question was not well formed. I'm not asking you if you could identify by name or face any particular opposing soldier. But were you able to tell from what unit or from what military force or organisation this attack was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Military organisation was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. What happened next in terms of those of you who were in the logistics building that you just described to us in the last few minutes, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: What did we do? We were there for a while, and then when they took the building, when the HVO took the building, with another five men, we fled across the rooftops to the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you able, in fact, to make it to and into the Vranica building, at least again, that portion which housed the ABiH 4th Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think we have heard a lot about this. Could you please lead this witness into the crucial points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You moved from the logistics component into that part of the Vranica building where the headquarters was located. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of avoiding private session, I'm not going to ask you these names now because I think the names will come up again in the future, in the future parts of your testimony anyway. But a number of those people who you named a few minutes ago, did they go with you, travel with you, if you will, from the logistics component to the headquarters component?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: We were altogether six. One was killed, and one was left behind or stayed behind from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness CC, to follow the President's guidance, would it be fair to say, then, as a summary, that you and the others then stayed in the Vranica building for the remaining part of the 9th of May, and that the attack continued around you during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And in addition, when you reached the Vranica building, can you tell the Chamber, were there also a number of civilians in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it was a civilian building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the morning of the 10th of May, did the artillery shelling begin again around 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Around 9.00 or 10.00 that morning, on the 10th of May, did anyone come to the building, or did you hear a voice or someone demanding that the occupants of the building surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you identify the person either by what you saw or heard or both that was making that demand at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. The person identified himself as the mayor of Mostar, Jadranko Topic, and commanded that we surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did the occupants of the Vranica building immediately surrender at that time? That is, when I say occupants, that is both the military personnel and the civilians. Did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: No. We remained there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, sometime after that, did you -- was there -- were there further demands that the occupants surrender coming from another person, that is coming from someone other than Jadranko Topic, the mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: A little later, as I recall, it was Juka who called on people to surrender. But that morning, it was Jadranko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you say "Juka" just now, is that a person perhaps more fully known as Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did you know, either then or did you come to know, of who Juka Prazina was in terms of his military position and role at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know, but later on I learned that he was with the Convicts ATG unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you know or come to know who Juka Prazina was subordinate to in terms of who his commanding officer was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Later on. At that time, I did not know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did you learn later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did you learn later on? Did you learn who his commanding officer was? And if you did, will you please tell the Chamber the name of that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: You mean the commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Mladen Naletilic, called Tuta, was his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how it is you heard that or how you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I personally heard it from Juka Prazina when he invited me to come over and join his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for the Chamber, we'll come to that sometime later in the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Going back to the 10th of May, after you saw -- after you heard Juka Prazina making this further demand that the occupants surrender, what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: We stayed on inside. There was -- the fire was still being --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I think it was Juka Prazina. And in fact, I'm not sure whether it was Juka or Jadranko, because this took place on the third floor. So I'm really not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Did there come a time shortly after that that, in fact, the occupants of the building did surrender and leave the Vranica building, around 2.00 on the 10th of May approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. Around 1400 hours, somewhere around that time, we came out and surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Witness just so there's no confusion about this and so the Chamber is clear, is it correct that some of the ABiH soldiers changed out of their uniforms into civilian clothes prior to the time that they surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, we changed into civilian clothes. In fact, all soldiers who were part of the brigade came out dressed as civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, as you came out of the Vranica building, did you see any soldiers or officers associated with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: When I came out, of course, they all gathered already. I saw Juka, I saw Zeljko Bosnjak. And Zeljko said to us, "You balijas thought you could keep us out?" I don't know what he meant. At that time, I did not know them, but later on, I came to know them all, during the time I spent in the camp at Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: During that time, in terms of the two men you just mentioned, Juka and Zeljko Bosnjak, did they identify or say anything that you overheard or was said to you that identified the unit that they were with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I did not know right away, I did not know about the convicts and Juka Prazina, because I had been in Mostar for a very brief period. But later on in Siroki Brijeg, I learned it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the question this way: After this date and in Siroki Brijeg and other places, did you continue to see these persons, Juka Prazina and Zeljko Bosnjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've always noticed the clock on the transcript is a bit different than the clock on the wall but the clock on the wall indicates it's 11.00, if you want to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before you start, Mr. Scott, there are two things I want to mention. The first one is to remind both parties we will start at 3.00 until 4.30 this afternoon because of the other obligations of the Judges during the lunch break. The second matter is that we are informed that medical examination of Mr. Naletilic will be performed on Thursday, November 1, 2001, from 12.00 noon to 2.00 in the afternoon at the Academic Medical Centre in Amsterdam. We believe this is a very important medical exam. So could we kindly ask the Defence counsel for Mr. Naletilic to allow us to sit in the morning without the presence of his client, in the morning session? Well, we understand that it is difficult for the Defence counsel to make the decision at this moment, but I hope that the both parties could discuss this matter during the lunch break. We understand it depends on which witness the Prosecutor is going to call on that day. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can tell you immediately, because I know, the position of my client. He does not want to interfere with the schedule of this trial in any way. I want to say something different. I wanted to accompany him this time to the hospital and talk to the doctors, but in that case, too, there will be no problem because my partner will be able to take over. If you want me to stay, however, I will go to Amsterdam another day. In any event, there will be no change of schedule on our behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. As for your accompanying your client to Amsterdam, I think we have to consult with the registrar about this matter. Thank you. So, Usher, would you please call in the witness? Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought it was the other Thursday. This Thursday, there will be no problem at all. I mean, I wanted to go to Amsterdam the other Thursday, not this Thursday. I thought it was the Thursday after this coming week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness CC, we were up to the point of time you and the others had come out of the Vranica building. You saw several individuals, including Juka Prazina and Zeljko Bosnjak. Around that time, did you see anyone else with Mr. Prazina that appeared to you to be doing something or identifying people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, when we were coming out of the Vranica building and when we were lined up, one of our soldiers was singled out by Juka and questioned as to who were the soldiers among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you identify for the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you identify for the Chamber who that particular soldier was who was singled out to identify people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. But do you want me to do that in open session or in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: If you feel more comfortable --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, can we go to private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are now in the open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness CC, my question to you, was there then a separation of various people who came out of the building into different groups and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, able-bodied men were separated on one side, and women and children on the other side. I didn't see that, but I heard Zeljko Bosnjak saying that Croat men and women should be separated into yet another group and released to go home. What happened next to those groups, I don't know. I only know what happened to our group, the group in which I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Before we get to that, can you tell the Chamber, is it correct that there were some journalists, some Croatian journalists, there including a TV crew from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. There was "Slobodan Dalmacija," the newspaper, and the state television from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the group of the men that you've told us about? The able-bodied men, I think you said. What happened to that group of people once you had left the building and been separated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, they lined us up there, and they took us away in the direction -- I don't know whether it was the mechanical engineering faculty or some ministry. I don't know because I don't know Mostar well. But they took us to this building. What kind of building it was, I really don't know. While they were taking us there, one of us was forced to carry Sefer's picture, and we were also made to sing some songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you say "Sefer's picture," you're referring to Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What kind of songs were you forced to sing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I think something like, "the smell of lilies pervading the fields," because it was Juka who expressly demanded that we sing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Well, when you say "lilies," does that have some particular symbolism that the Chamber -- you might be able to help the Chamber with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I think so, because lilies were our emblem. It was on our military emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you say your emblem, you're talking about the Bosniaks or the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I mean the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you say you were taken to this building, is it accurate that you walked for some seven or ten minutes approximately to this further location?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I believe that's a leading and suggestive question, and I'm going to object on that ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It is a leading question. Would you please rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. President, and based on what the Court's told me, I'm going to continue to lead where -- I'm going to continue if I think it's not a critical item. Of course, counsel can object, but you've told me, Mr. President, to try to be quicker. If we certainly come to something where one of the accused is directly involved, I can assure the Chamber I will change, but I'm trying to abide by the Court's direction. I don't think it's particularly critical that they walked for seven or ten minutes. But be that as it may, I will ask the witness an open-ended question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how long it took you approximately to get from the Vranica building to this second location where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: About ten minutes or so. We didn't check the time but it was ten minutes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you got to this location, did you see any -- what appeared to be HVO officials or officers there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. There I saw a large number of soldiers. At that time I didn't know anyone, but I came to know them later. I saw Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta; I saw Basic, I saw Misic. And there were other soldiers, too. In any event, there were a lot of troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you around this time see or hear people addressing this individual called Tuta? And if so, can you share with the Chamber anything you heard them say or how it was that they addressed this Tuta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, they addressed him. Misic addressed him. Somebody said that we should be executed at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll come to that in just a moment. Do you recall how Tuta was dressed -- this person that you said was Tuta, how he was dressed at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I remember. He was wearing a uniform. He had a Motorola, with which he immediately hit Alica Pobric, and he hit another man as well. I don't know that other man. I just heard him saying, "Why me? We went to school together." And he said, "Precisely, that's why."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Before we come back to what you just now told us, if you allow me, before you get to that point, you've now told us a couple of things. You said there was also a statement about some of you being executed. Now, tell us more about that. What happened and what was said, in terms of whether some of you should be executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, this was expressly demanded by Misic and Tuta, that we should be executed at once, while Basic and Juka opposed them, defending us. They said that was not the place for us to be executed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you recall Juka saying anything to you about - sorry, not to you - Juka saying anything around that time about needing you as prisoners to exchange for other of his -- others of his unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. Juka did say that he can't execute us because he has his own soldiers in Zenica that he needs to get in exchange for us, that we were his prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, you already told us that you saw a couple of prisoners or so being -- being beaten.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Alica Pobric and that man. And I got a blow from Juka. I don't know why. Because the commotion started when execution was mentioned, a commotion among Juka and the other people from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Witness CC, give me a moment, please, just to check the transcript on something. You said -- just so the record is clear, you've mentioned, in this exchange about you being -- some of you being executed, you mentioned four names, Misic, Tuta, Juka and another individual, a fourth individual, and I'm not sure the transcript is correct. Can you name that fourth individual again? One of the ones who you said opposed you being executed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I don't know his first name, but I heard his last name was Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, now, moving beyond Mr. Pobric being hit, you said that you saw and heard a second person, perhaps, and maybe a third. I'm not sure; I'm about to ask you. Who else did you see being hit after Mr. Pobric was hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Just when we arrived outside that building, we were in a file. We were lined up. Tuta came carrying a Motorola, and he immediately hit Pobric. And then they removed him slightly from us. I believe Juka was with him, and then I saw him on the edge of my field of vision. You didn't dare really look around because we were ordered to look down. But we did look, and I saw when a man of medium height, 170 centimetres perhaps, blond with a small beard, get hit. And I heard that man saying, "Why me, when we went to school together?" And I heard Tuta saying, "Precisely, that's why." But I didn't see anything else. Then, guns were pulled out, and a shot was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Witness CC, let me go back for one moment before we get too far ahead. You said -- a moment ago, you said that as soon as Tuta struck Pobric, that Juka came up and, you said, "removed him slightly from us." Can you tell us more about what you saw Juka do in that regard and if you saw or could see where Pobric was taken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, he remained there close to us. He wasn't taken away anywhere. He remained in proximity. But I believe Juka protected him. Juka was protecting Alica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Proceeding on, then, was a group of you then taken on a bus, placed on a bus, and taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. When they rejected the possibility of execution, Tuta personally said, "Balijas can go to Listica. Who said they couldn't?" And then they ordered buses to come and take us to Listica, that is, Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you taken to Siroki Brijeg -- were you taken then to the MUP or Ministry of Interior station there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken on a bus outside the MUP building where we were also lined up once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: We were questioned there about names, and they started beating Goran Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you identify, if you're able to, the particular person who was beating Goran Zekic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I can't say. It was none of those there. It was a simple soldier. The chief of MUP, Cane, was present. I know that because I used to work in the MUP. I just know the man's nickname. It was Cane. He was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And after you were initially taken off the bus and this beating -- this initial beating occurred, were you then put into some sort of a prison or holding facility there in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. We were placed in two cells. We were taken to two cells where we were crammed like sardines in a can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Could you tell or did you come to know during the time that you were held there who was in charge of that facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Cane was in charge of the police administration. He was the chief, which means he was in charge of that police station. Whether he had a superior role, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask the usher's assistance, please, if the witness could please be shown 26.6, 26.7, and 26.8. If those could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you can first look at 26.6. Do you recognise what's depicted or shown in that photograph? And if you do, can you please tell the Chamber what it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entrance down into the cell in the basement, the cell where we were placed. From the corridor, you went to the basement, and downstairs in the basement were the cells, below the level of that floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: This was in the MUP station in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Siroki Brijeg police station of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior. Those were the stairs down which we climbed to get into the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Will you look, please, at 26.7. What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Those are the cells where we spent time, where we were locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And there were approximately 18 of you in this cell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber, when the time -- forgive me. At the time that you were held there, did it look like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: No, no, it didn't look like this. It was much worse. It was dirty. It wasn't clean at all. There were no cots. There were no blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you next look at 26.8.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the other cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The photographs can be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The day after this, were some of the prisoners that you were travelling with at that time or being held with, were some of them taken to work somewhere in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, we were taken to work at the swimming pool. The town swimming pool, that's where we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was that took you to that location? How were you guarded or taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the civilian police who took us there. It was a long time ago, really. But we were guarded by the drivers of the trucks that carried the waste and the branches and all the litter that we gathered and loaded on to the trucks. Those drivers guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And did you work at the swimming pool on just the one occasion or can you give the Chamber some idea of approximately how many times you worked there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: In those seven days I spent there, I went to that swimming pool only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention back into the holding area itself, can you tell us about whether you saw a man there named Romeo Blazevic? And what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: That was in the evening. The doors to the cells opened and a soldier - I had seen him once before near the Vranica building in a coffee bar, but I did not know who he was - so he burst in and started beating people. He had a rod with a metal ball at the top, and with that rod or stick, he started beating people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I received a blow. I was near the door. I was not hit in the head, but rather on the body and on the back, but people who were further inside, who -- he could swing freely and hit people. He broke people's heads, like Goran Zekic's, and also he fractured somebody's arm as they tried to defend themselves. Then he pulled out a pistol and put it into people's mouth, and blood was spurting all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Directing your attention a few days further, was there a time when some HVO soldiers came to the cell again during the night? And what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. He did come. I did not know that then, but later I worked for that man, Ivan Hrkac, called Cikota. In fact, I don't know if he had adopted that name or not, but his real name was Ivan Hrkac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, this may be a point where you can assist the Chamber. Did you know this Ivan Cikota to be the brother of a man named Mario Cikota?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a brother of Mario Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber please whether this brother, Mario Cikota, had been killed sometime previous to the date you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, Mario was killed before. I did not know that, but he told us that his brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When you say "he" just now, you're referring to Ivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to Ivan, because a dead man cannot talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Of course. And what was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: That is, Mario could not have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I think we can agree with that, Witness. Can you spell for the record, so the record is clear, the last name of these two brothers, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: H-r-k-a-c. H-r-k-a-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you know at that time, or come to know, that this brother, Ivan Cikota, or Ivan, I should say, Hrkac, after his brother died, began to also use the nickname Cikota?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. I also heard soldiers who were around him, who came with him when he came to beat us and later on when I worked for him, I also heard them referring to him as Cikota.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for your assistance on that. This person now that you've identified, Ivan Cikota, he came -- he was one of these people who came into the cell, into the cell area, the holding area, on the evening you began to tell us about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They opened the door and said, "You, you and you, come out."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Then these men would come out of the cell. There was something like a kitchen area there, and this is where they beat these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: If you can, do you remember the names of any of the individuals who were beaten around that time or that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you say, please?
