I think the "reservoir" is deceptive but I think that may be a word you used. Can you point on that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you, please, to take a marker and mark a number 1 on the location where you say you worked on the canal in connection with Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, this is where the reservoir was. And from there, water was to be run over to Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Two questions then to follow up on that. When you say reservoir -- at least maybe a cultural or language matter, Witness CC, I admit. When I hear the word "reservoir", I typically think of a surface -- a pond or a lake. Was there a surface pond or lake there, or are you talking about a reservoir being like a spring or a well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: No, it's not like a lake, no. It would be something similar to a pool from where you would pump water and send it somewhere else. So that is what we in Bosnia called a reservoir or cistern.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: All right. And my final question to you: From the vantage point where you were working on the canal that you have just marked, at least in part, as being depicted at location number 1, could you see Tuta's house from that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I don't recall being able to. But from the end of the canal here, from that vantage point, I could see it because we went digging from there uphill. And when we approached this area by bus, there was a part of the road where there was an opening. And so from there, I could see Tuta's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: I guess I do have one final question, then: From what you've told us then, can you show on this photograph -- can you see Tuta's house, or what was described to you by the soldiers as Tuta's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Please point that out on the map, and would you place a number 2 at that location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness CC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness, I wonder if you can help me with this: You told us earlier on in your testimony that you really didn't know any of the personalities involved with the conflict in Mostar on the 9th of May; but during your period of detention, you came to know who they all were. Now, I'm particularly interested in this man whose name is Juka Prazina. You described how he called upon the civilians and the soldiers in the Vranica building to surrender. And then you described how he was with a number of other people who appeared to be leaders that day. Did you ever see this Juka Prazina again after the 9th of May in any of the detention centres where you were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I saw him but not at the camp. When we were going back from Ljubuski, he boarded a bus and he asked who would volunteer into his unit. The second time I saw him was at Zeljko Bosnjak, and the third time I saw him was at Ivan Cikota's. Personally he offered me 20.000 German marks to come and join him. And three prisoners went with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What was his position in the unit? You described the unit. Do you know what the unit was and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of that unit. That was an anti-terrorist unit attached to the Convicts Battalion. That is how -- what they said. He was personally subordinate to Tuta, because he told me, "I can bring you out, just come join me, and Tuta will agree to that." Now you're reminding me of this. I know that Juka was subordinate to Tuta, and his unit was an ATG. It was probably a special-purpose unit. I'm not a military analyst to know these things. But he was fairly well known, he and his unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of his unit, his ATG unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: No, I only knew about that acronym, ATG or AT -- that is an acronym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you learn anything more about this man, Mr. Prazina? Was he a local man from Mostar? Was he a career soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I knew that he was from Sarajevo. He told us that he was from Sarajevo. And he was a career soldier. In fact, he was like a mercenary soldier. He worked for money. Because he came from Sarajevo to Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: What I meant when I said a career soldier, I meant somebody who joined as an officer and gone through cadet school and spent years working his way up through the ranks as an officer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I don't know if he was schooled, but he identified himself as a general, and supposedly general of the ABiH. I really don't know whether he went through officers' training. But when he -- but when Rahimic was forced to carry around the picture of General Halilovic, then -- of Sefer Halilovic, then he said, "You see, I was supposed to be this. I should have been this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So are you saying, Witness, that Juka Prazina was a Bosniak and had been in the ABiH previously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was. Whether he was Bosniak, I really don't know. He probably was. He never said that he was a Bosniak. He said that he had been -- I don't know. I only arrived in Mostar in 1993, and joined the army, but I don't know whether he had been in the army before. But if he saw himself as somebody who should have been a general, then I assume that he had some officer training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was that a slip of the tongue when you said that he had been in the ABiH? Did you mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: No. I don't know whether he was with the JNA in 1992. That is what I meant. I really don't know whether he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you these questions is that this man, Mr. Prazina, appeared to be able to overrule Mr. Tuta in relation to execution of your group. And I wanted you to clarify that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: I personally think -- I overheard all this conversation. I really believe that Juka did help us at that time because -- I did not say this before, but one always remembers some -- when we were there in front of this ministry, somebody fired a shot and a man was wounded in the leg, and Juka stepped in and protected us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And you also said that he protected Mr. Pobric, who was being attacked by Tuta.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. He did protect him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Now, the next question that I wanted to ask you was about your mention of the Geneva Convention. That was in relation to Mr. Jahic. Who in particular asked him to sign a document stating that he had been treated in accordance with the Geneva Convention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: That we all were treated, all the prisoners who were going from Siroki Brijeg to Ljubuski, and that was the civilian police. They took him there, and it was them who demanded that of him. I think that Cane was present. But it was demanded by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Were you visited by any representative of either the UN or the Red Cross while you were in Siroki Brijeg or the short time that you were in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Never, not -- not until we came to the Heliodrom. Whenever we were -- throughout the time at the Siroki Brijeg, whenever they would come, they would hide us so we had no contact with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that representatives from the Red Cross came but that you were hidden from them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Yes. I personally saw them, but we were never brought in front of them. We were always hidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why you were retransferred from Ljubuski to Siroki Brijeg, your whole group? Do you have any idea why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Eighteen of us were transferred back to Siroki Brijeg in order to finish the work on the swimming pool. When we came -- when we were brought back, they had extra work for us. I think that that was the reason. I don't know of any other reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did your group have particular building and construction skills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CC
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. [redacted]. There were carpenters. There were painters. There were people who could do a lot of other things in construction business. In fact, there was even a foreman. I think (redacted), I think that he was -- had training in construction, so he was a technician. So we were skilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: They were all the questions I wanted to put to you, so I thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, witness. Thank you for helping us by giving your evidence. When the blind is pulled down, you may leave now. We wish you all good luck. While the witness is leaving --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for intervening in this way but before the passage of the transcript too quickly, I think there needs to be one redaction. There was a protected witness's name that was just mentioned, if that could be just redacted. It's in approximately line 20 on page 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I didn't notice that. Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender my exhibits now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sure, after Mr. Prosecutor. Yes. At this stage, Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, all of the exhibits themselves, that is the underlying exhibits, had previously been admitted. However, I think this witness marked three versions, and I'll ask the registrar to assist me on that, but he marked a version of 25.2, he marked a version of 33.2 and 33.5. So only as to those additional marked versions, we offer those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The -- we have no objections to the photographs that were marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have any documents to tender at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is P11.18. This would be the Defence exhibit D1/28. And then in order, P26.2, and then the Prosecution Exhibit P26.9, in order. And that's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any marks by this witness for all those documents? I understand all those documents have been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. All those documents are admitted into the evidence. And Madam Registrar will give each a proper number. There's two things I would like to remind both parties at this stage. Last Friday when we finished the testimony of that religious official, the Prosecutor tendered a bundle of documents. And then, Mr. Krsnik, you told us that you did not object to some of them, but you are objecting to others. Since there are a lot of documents, this Trial Chamber asked you to provide us a simple list stating which documents you are objecting and which you are not, without the reason why you object to those documents. We have not been furnished with this list at this moment, and we are expecting your list on Thursday. Otherwise, all those documents will be admitted into evidence automatically. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have to say that the Defence counsel did furnish the Registry yesterday with the document, and it was filed yesterday. So the distribution probably took place this morning or this afternoon, and you should, therefore, have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another matter is that because of the trial schedule of the other cases, and the rearrangement of the courtroom on Thursday, 25th of October, we will start out sitting at 9.30 in the morning, and we will have lunch break at 1.00 p.m. But in the afternoon, we have to start the afternoon sitting at 2.00 until 3.30.
